data TOCEntry = TOCEntry
  {tocKey :: !Word16, offset :: !Word16, blocks :: !Word16}
  deriving (Show)

data Op
  = Op_0x00_xyz !Int16 !Int16 !Int16
  | Op_0x01_xyz !Int16 !Int16 !Int16
  | Op_0x02_vertex {x :: !Int16, y :: !Int16, z :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x03 {angle :: !Int16, len1 :: !Int16, len2 :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x05 {var :: !Word16, int1 :: !Int32, int2 :: !Int32}
  | Op_0x0a_toc ![TOCEntry]
  | Op_0x0b_jump_rel !Int
  | Op_0x0c_set_fill_color !Word16
  | Op_0x0d_load {loadKey :: !Word16, readOfs :: !Word16, d5 :: !Word8}
  | Op_0x12_set_fill_color !Word16
  | Op_0x16_set_fill_color !Word8 !Word8 !Word8 !Word8 !Word16 !Word16 !Word16
  | Op_0x17_set_fill_color !Word8 !Word8 !Word8 !Word8 !Word16 !Word16 !Word16
  | Op_0x18_call !Int16
  | Op_0x19_return
  | Op_0x1a_copy_word {varTgt :: !Word16, varSrc :: !Word16}
  | Op_0x1b_set_fill_color_5
  | Op_0x1c_set_fill_color_2
  | Op_0x1d {cmp :: !Word16, long1 :: !Word32, long2 :: !Word32}
  | Op_0x1e {size :: !Word16}
  | Op_0x1f_call !Int16
  | Op_0x20_jump_if_outside1 {ofs :: !Word16, var :: !Word16, lwb :: !Int16, upb :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x21_jump_if_outside2
      { ofs :: !Word16,
        var1 :: !Word16,
        lwb1 :: !Int16,
        upb1 :: !Int16,
        var2 :: !Word16,
        lwb2 :: !Int16,
        upb2 :: !Int16
      }
  | Op_0x23_jump_unless
      { ofs :: !Word16,
        var :: !Word16,
        mask :: !Word16
      }
  | Op_0x24_coord_frame {scale :: !Int16, x :: !Int16, y :: !Int16, z :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x25_write_word
      { var :: !Word16,
        to :: !Word16
      }
  | Op_0x28_jump_if_compare {op :: !Word16, ofs :: !Word16, var1 :: !Word16, var2 :: !Word16}
  | Op_0x29_draw_end
  | Op_0x2a_true
  | Op_0x2b !Int16 !Int16 !Int16 !Int16 !Int16 !Int16 !Int16
  | Op_0x2f_draw_begin
  | Op_0x31_vertex_idx {idx :: !Word16, x :: !Int16, y :: !Int16, z :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x32_load_vertex {idx :: !Word16}
  | Op_0x33_fill_poly {idx :: !Word16}
  | Op_0x34_jump_if_outside3 {ofs :: !Word16, z :: !Int16, x :: !Int16, delta :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x37_coord_frame {scale :: !Int16, x :: !Int16, y :: !Int16, z :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x39_set_palette_entry !Word16 !Word16
  | Op_0x40_vertex_2d {x :: !Int16, z :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x41_vertex_2d {x :: !Int16, z :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x42_jump_if_outside_box {ofs :: !Word16, minX :: !Int16, maxX :: !Int16, minZ :: !Int16, maxZ :: !Int16}
  | Op_0x43_jump_if_not_in_range {ofs :: !Word16, px :: Int32, py :: Int32, pz :: Int32, alpha :: !Word16, dx :: !Word32, dy :: !Word32, dz :: !Word32}
  | Op_0x79_end
  | OpOther !Word8
  deriving (Show)

parseTOCEntry :: G.Get TOCEntry
parseTOCEntry = return TOCEntry `ap` G.getWord16be `ap` G.getWord16be `ap` G.getWord16be

parseOp :: G.Get Op
parseOp = do
  G.getInt8
  op <- G.getWord8
  case op of
    0x0 -> do
      x <- G.getInt16be
      y <- G.getInt16be
      z <- G.getInt16be
      return $ Op_0x00_xyz x y z
    0x01 -> do
      x <- G.getInt16be
      y <- G.getInt16be
      z <- G.getInt16be
      return $ Op_0x01_xyz x y z
    0x02 ->
      return Op_0x02_vertex
        `ap` B.getInt16be
        `ap` B.getInt16be
        `ap` B.getInt16be
    0x03 ->
      return Op_0x03
        `ap` B.getInt16be
        `ap` B.getInt16be
        `ap` B.getInt16be
    0x05 ->
      return Op_0x05 `ap` G.getWord16be `ap` G.getInt32be `ap` G.getInt32be
    0x0a -> do
      ofs <- G.getWord16be
      records <- mapM (const parseTOCEntry) [0 .. (ofs - 4) `div` 6 - 1]
      return $ Op_0x0a_toc records
    0x0b -> do
      ofs <- G.getInt16be
      return $ Op_0x0b_jump_rel $ fromIntegral ofs
    0x0c ->
      return Op_0x0c_set_fill_color
        `ap` B.getWord16be
    0x0d -> do
      key <- G.getWord16be
      readOfs <- G.getWord16be
      G.getWord8
      d5 <- G.getWord8
      return $ Op_0x0d_load key readOfs d5
    0x12 ->
      return Op_0x12_set_fill_color
        `ap` G.getWord16be
    0x16 ->
      return Op_0x16_set_fill_color
        `ap` G.getWord8

# Patterns

## Overview

Patterns contain the actual musical event data (notes, meta events, etc.). Each track points to its pattern data via a pattern pointer stored in the track header.

## Pattern Data Structure

Pattern data consists of a sequence of **6-byte events**. Events are read sequentially until an end marker is encountered.

## Event Format

All events are **6 bytes** in length:

```
Byte 0: Note/Event identifier
Byte 1: Status byte
Byte 2-3: Position (16-bit big-endian)
Byte 4: Velocity/Parameter
Byte 5: Duration/Argument
```

### Position (Bytes 2-3)
- **Format**: 16-bit big-endian unsigned integer
- **Range**: 0x0000 - 0xFFFF
- **Units**: Ticks (relative to pattern start or absolute, depending on context)
- **Purpose**: Timing position of event within pattern

## Event Types

### Note On/Off Events
- **Status**: `0x90` or `0x91` (Note On)
- **Byte 0**: MIDI note number (0-127)
- **Byte 1**: `0x90` or `0x91`
- **Byte 2-3**: Position in ticks
- **Byte 4**: Velocity + 2 (if velocity > 0, subtract 2 to get actual velocity)
  - `velocity = byte4 - 2` if `byte4 > 2`
  - `byte4 = 0` indicates Note Off
- **Byte 5**: Duration or additional parameter

**Note**: Velocity is stored as `actual_velocity + 2`. A value of `0` in byte 4 indicates Note Off.

### Meta Events (0x70)
- **Status**: `0x70`
- **Byte 0**: Event identifier (varies)
- **Byte 1**: `0x70` (meta event marker)
- **Byte 2**: Type/position parameter
- **Byte 3**: Parameter 1 (0x00 = standard, 0x80 = control)
- **Byte 4**: Parameter 2 (sub-type: 0x03, 0x05, 0x09, 0x11)
- **Byte 5**: Additional argument

**Common Patterns**:
- `[0x00, 0x03]` - Most common meta event
- `[0x00, 0x05]` - Specific event type
- `[0x00, 0x09]` - Possible tempo-related
- `[0x00, 0x11]` - Possible tempo-related
- `[0x80, 0x00]` - Control flag

### Time Signature Change Events
See [Time Signature Changes](04-time-signature.md) section for details.

### End of Pattern Marker
- **Status**: `0xFC` or `0xFD`
- **Purpose**: Indicates end of pattern data
- **Byte 0**: `0x7F` or event identifier
- **Byte 1**: `0xFC` (end marker) or `0xFD` (section marker)
- **Bytes 2-5**: May contain end position or padding

### Structural Events
- **Bar Marker**: `NOTE=0x82, STATUS=0x00`
- **Section Boundary**: `NOTE=0x80, STATUS=0x00`
- **Padding Events**: Various NOTE values (0xB7-0xBF) with varying STATUS

## Reading Pattern Data

1. **Get Pattern Pointer**: Read from track header at offset `+0x14` (32-bit BE)
2. **Navigate to Offset**: Jump to absolute file offset specified by pattern pointer
3. **Read Events**: Read 6-byte events sequentially
4. **Check Status**: Examine byte 1 to determine event type
5. **Parse Event**: Extract data based on event type
6. **Continue**: Move to next event (offset += 6)
7. **Stop**: When end marker (`0xFC` or `0xFD`) is encountered

## Pattern Data Layout

```
Pattern Data (starts at pattern pointer)
├── Event 0 (6 bytes)
│   ├── Note/ID
│   ├── Status
│   ├── Position (16-bit)
│   ├── Velocity/Param
│   └── Duration/Arg
├── Event 1 (6 bytes)
│   └── ...
├── Event 2 (6 bytes)
│   └── ...
└── End Marker (0xFC or 0xFD)
```

## Position Calculation

Position values are stored as 16-bit big-endian integers representing ticks. The relationship to musical time depends on:
- PPQ value from header (typically 192)
- Time signature (affects beats per measure)
- Tempo (affects ticks per second)

**Example**:
- PPQ = 192
- Time signature = 4/4
- Position = 192 ticks = 1 quarter note = 1 beat

## Notes

- All events are exactly 6 bytes
- Events are read sequentially until end marker
- Position is relative to pattern start (or absolute, verify with your implementation)
- Velocity is stored as `actual_velocity + 2` for Note On events
- Pattern data can contain various event types mixed together
- End markers (`0xFC`, `0xFD`) terminate pattern reading

# Original-style Pascal recovery and execution

## What was actually recovered

The original has a Borland runtime marker, Pascal shortstrings, callee-cleaned
16-bit calls, hidden static links, and compatible runtime/file layouts. This
supports a Turbo/Borland Pascal-family origin, **not an exact compiler version**.
No original `.PAS`/unit/debug names or author source files were identified by the
bounded inspection described in [pascal-layouts.md](pascal-layouts.md).

The reconstruction now contains:

- `pascal/LZCORE.PAS`: six operations in Pascal, including packed records,
  original-style `var` parameter order and genuinely nested helpers. Three
  outer facades supply unrecovered parent/global context; they are explicitly
  not the original complete enclosing procedures.
- `pascal/LZRLE.PAS`: the original-style unsafe decompressor at `0x182d0`.
- `pascal/LZTYPES.PAS`: sixteen measured storage layouts, plus documented array
  views. Names, grouping and Pascal declaration spelling are analyst choices.
  Unknown bytes remain real fields rather than discarded padding.
- `LZBRIDGE.PAS` and `LZRLEBR.PAS`: **modern native test bridges**, not original
  game units or DOS-compatible external ABIs.
- `LZPROBE.PAS`: a **new computational verification program**, not a recovered
  main program, game launcher, or playable game.

The prior C reconstruction remains available as a separate representation.
Pascal verification executes original machine instructions; C is not its oracle.

## Compiling and running

Use Free Pascal **3.2.2**. A packaged native `fpc` may use its normal configuration.
For a standalone installation, set `FPC` to the compiler executable and `FPC_RTL`
to the directory containing `system.ppu`. For the DOS cross compiler, set:

```sh
export FPC_DOS=/absolute/path/to/lib/fpc/3.2.2/ppcross8086
export FPC_DOS_RTL=/absolute/path/to/lib/fpc/3.2.2/units/msdos/8086-compact/rtl
make pascal-native PYTHON=.venv/bin/python
make pascal-dos PYTHON=.venv/bin/python
.venv/bin/python -m pytest tests -q
```

`tools/build_pascal.py` resolves explicit variables, then PATH, then the known
optional reference-workspace installation if present. It verifies compiler
version and output magic, uses separate generated-unit directories, and never
changes global configuration. `FPC_UNITS`, `FPC8086`, and `FPC8086_UNITS` remain
supported aliases for the initial core-test configuration. The RLE host test uses
`FPC`/`FPC_RTL`; prefer those canonical names for all components.

The [toolchain manifest](../analysis/pascal-toolchain.json) pins the official
retrieved native/cross archives, sizes and SHA-256s. The CI workflow shows the
hash-checked extraction of only the cross compiler and compact-model units.
Compilers, archives, generated units, libraries and EXEs are not committed.

The DOS flags are `-Mtp -Tmsdos -WmCompact -XX`. The measured compact build has
`Integer=2`, `Word=2`, `LongInt=4`, `Pointer=4`; the native TP-mode probe has
`2,2,4,8`. Small-model DOS data pointers were only two bytes, so that model was
not used for the final far-data tests. Matching pointer width does **not** make
FPC output binary-compatible with the original compiler. `-XX` accommodates the
archive's smartlinked `system.a` runtime.

`make pascal-native` builds two host shared libraries and an executed probe.
`make pascal-dos` builds `build/pascal-dos/LZPROBE.EXE` and executes its actual
MZ-relocated instructions in Unicorn. Failure, unknown DOS services, or exhausted
instruction budget is a nonzero result. The Python tests also compare that
program's results with original instructions, not just a hardcoded PASS banner.

## Verification layers — do not conflate them

1. **Native Pascal versus original DOS instructions:** the unchanged six-routine
   oracle corpus performs **173,725 comparisons**. It covers every signed-word
   friction input, byte arithmetic boundaries, buffer/state output and collection
   quirks. The actual original runtime stack guard executes; code remains protected
   and unchanged. See [pascal-core.md](pascal-core.md).
2. **Native Pascal RLE versus original DOS instructions:** **1,052 comparisons**:
   256 controls times four requested lengths, plus seven levels times two planes
   times two controlled memory tails. This is a bounded, non-segment-wrapping
   arena contract, not every possible pointer/count combination.
3. **Newly compiled i8086 DOS execution:** `tests/test_pascal_probe.py` runs the
   rebuilt MZ with a limited DOS-service fixture. Its seven routines are compared
   against **12 original invocations** (including five friction values and two
   RLE requests). This is a small cross-target execution check, not a claim that
   all 174,777 native differential comparisons ran on the i8086 build.
4. **Compiled type layouts:** sixteen sizes plus selected field offsets are
   measured in both native and actually executed DOS builds. Odd-position words,
   actor byte `$05`, Pascal `string[8]`, and the known 45-byte score prefix are
   retained. The 46-byte separation between two globals is not falsely asserted
   as the record's size. `TFile128` is an original-runtime view, not FPC's file type.
5. Existing C/evidence/asset tests remain regression coverage, not substitutes for
   the Pascal checks. Optional DOS tests skip only if no cross compiler exists;
   an explicitly configured but broken compiler/RTL fails instead.

## The DOS execution fixture is deliberately limited

`tools/run_dos_probe.py` is **not a full DOS emulator**. Unicorn executes the
compiled guest's instructions. The fixture supplies a synthetic PSP/environment,
conventional-memory area, and only the observed INT 21h services: version 5.0,
get/set interrupt vector, standard-handle device query, unsupported-LFN response,
stdout/stderr writes, and exit. The DOS version is fixture input, not an observed
host OS. There is no guest filesystem, BIOS/VGA/audio hardware, real timer,
keyboard, or gameplay validation. It does not execute original game startup.

## Unsafe decompressor compatibility

The recovered Pascal deliberately retains these observed behaviors:

- `PackedLength` is unused; input is consumed until enough output is produced.
- Each triplet supplies two nibble run lengths plus two values; both lengths add
  one, but each store loop also includes its upper endpoint.
- Consequently a run stores an extra byte; the next run can overlap that store.
- The first run executes even when `Required=0`.
- All fourteen real level planes underfill and can read beyond their payload.
  The tests put the payload in controlled arenas and compare the actual memory
  consequences with original execution. They do not invent missing level bytes.

`LegacyExpandUnsafe` must not be used as an untrusted-input asset decoder. The
separate Python decoder remains bounded and rejects underfilled output. The host
bridge and tests require sufficiently allocated, non-overlapping arenas without
16-bit offset wrap; invalid pointers and exhausted storage are outside scope.

## REA assembly presentation corrections

A narrow independent decoder of opcode `8C/8E` plus register-direct ModRM found
**23 mismatches among 65 checked instructions**. For example, original bytes
`8e da` at `0x19203` and `0x19b21` load DS from DX, whereas retained REA text
reverses the operands. `8e c0` at `0x107d2` similarly loads ES from AX.

The audit is reproduced by:

```sh
.venv/bin/python tools/audit_segment_moves.py
```

Its complete result is [segment-register-audit.json](../analysis/segment-register-audit.json).
Raw REA dossiers, assembly and pseudocode are preserved unchanged. This is only
an audit of unprefixed 16-bit register-direct segment MOVs, **not a validation of
all other rendered operands or all decompiler semantics**. Original bytes and
actual instruction execution take precedence.

## Still unrecovered

Original identifiers, exact source syntax, unit names, compiler release/options,
full parent procedures and globals, main loop, complete actor physics/rendering,
audio/input/interrupt behavior, DOS integration, and exact level-tail memory state
remain unresolved. This work recovers a tested original-language subset and
storage structure; it is neither the author's source archive nor a complete or
bit-identical DOS game rebuild.

# Engine Architecture

Pizza Legacy is a new C++20 engine written from scratch to reproduce the
original game's behavior while providing a modern, portable way to play it.
It is not a decompilation or port of the original engine; it was developed
through a combination of gameplay observation, asset file analysis, and study
of the disassembled DOS executable.

## Original asset format support

The engine parses the original 1994 asset formats:

- **BOB sprites** with animation sequences
- **VGA graphics** with indexed-color palettes
- **FNT bitmap fonts**
- **CMF music** (Creative Music Format, OPL3 FM synthesis via libADLMIDI)
- **VOC audio** (Creative Voice Format, decoded and resampled to stereo)
- City map data, pizza recipes, restaurant layouts, and character data from
  original formats (English version only)

All assets are loaded on demand through a template-based `ResourceManager<T, Loader>`
that caches resources by filename.

## Type-safe coordinate systems

The engine uses phantom types to make coordinate spaces distinct at compile
time. `WorldPoint`, `ViewPoint`, and `ScreenPoint` are separate types that
cannot be accidentally mixed. Camera and viewport transforms convert between
them explicitly. This is zero-cost: the types have the same runtime
representation as their underlying data (e.g. int). The same pattern is used
for IDs (players, restaurants, cities) to prevent mix-ups.

## Rendering pipeline

Rendering uses a layered composition model with per-layer dirty tracking:

- Each view implements a `Renderable` interface with dirty-state tracking
- Layers are cached to SDL surfaces and only recomposed when marked dirty
- 8-bit indexed-color surfaces are expanded to RGBA during composition
- A CRT scaling mode upscales the native 640x400 to 640x480 to approximate
  the original CRT aspect ratio

Screens are managed as a stack, with an overlay system composited on top.
Popups, tooltips, and a debug layer are all independent
overlays that can block or pass through input to the view beneath them.
Screen transitions use palette-based fade-out/fade-in.

## Input system

Input is abstracted into two layers: physical keys (SDL backend) and semantic
actions (game-level). Key bindings support chords (e.g. Ctrl+Shift+B) and are
fully configurable (though not through a UI yet). Listeners register for
actions with priority ordering, and an IME-aware text input mode uses RAII
tokens for safe session management. Continuous axes are computed from input
sources to support keyboard and gamepad input.

## Interaction and UI framework

Mouse interaction is based on rectangular hit regions registered with
callbacks, per layer. Events include enter/leave/hover, click, double-click,
scrolling and drag-and-drop. Registration uses RAII tokens for automatic
cleanup. Tooltips, custom cursors, and exclusive capture modes are built in.

## Audio

The audio system mixes sound effects in real time and plays music through OPL3
FM synthesis. VOC samples are decoded from 8-bit mono to 16-bit stereo
(duplicated channels). Separate volume controls for master, music, and effects,
with gain control.

## Debug console and asset viewers

A built-in debug console accepts commands at runtime for inspecting and
manipulating game state. The engine also ships with dedicated viewer modes for
the original asset formats (sprites, graphics, fonts, palettes, sounds),
launchable via CLI flags, used for helping reverse engineering the original
game's data files.

## Cross-platform

Binary releases are available for Windows, Linux, macOS, and Haiku. The engine
is designed to be highly portable and should build on most modern desktop platforms
with SDL3 support, including the BSDs and other Unix-like systems.

Only the primary release platforms are regularly tested, so support for BSD and
other secondary platforms is currently best-effort, but portability is a major
project goal and platform-specific code is kept to a minimum.

Save data and configuration files are stored in the appropriate user data
directories for each platform; the only external files accessed are the
original game assets from the directory you selected.
